name: Mongolian cheek spots

card.summary: A historical practice in which royal Mongolian women painted red spots on the cheeks below the eyes, a rosy cosmetic look.
card.note: Very thinly documented; origin and meaning are unclear.

quick.overview:
Mongolian cheek spots refers to red spots that women of royal families are said to have painted at the centre of each cheek, just under the eyes. It is a blush-style look: colour placed high on the cheek for a flushed, healthy appearance.

The practice is documented in only a brief passage of general cosmetics history. The reason for it is described there as a mystery, with one account calling red cheeks a sign of a happy queen [1].
quick.how: The look is a round dab of red pigment on the cheekbone area, as the historical description gives. Modern interest is mostly as a makeup-history reference for placement of blush.
quick.risks: No risks are documented. The historical source is thin, so details should be treated as tentative.

lead: Mongolian cheek spots are a cosmetic custom in which women of royal families painted red spots at the centre of their cheeks, just beneath the eyes [1]. The look adds a focal point of colour high on the face, similar in effect to blush.

Wikipedia's history of cosmetics notes that the reason for the practice is a mystery, and that one account says red cheeks signified a happy queen; that passage rests on a makeup blog rather than scholarly work [1]. No clinical or ethnographic studies are known on the subject.

angle.text: Painted red spots add visible colour to the cheek area, giving a flushed, youthful look in the manner of blush. The sources are historical and brief.
